I would like to make closing remarks in my capacity as chair of the 25th session of the Permanent Forum. Distinguished members of the Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues, distinguished observers from member states, indigenous peoples organizations, and the intergovernmental system, non-governmental organizations, the academia, and the media. Indigenous brothers and sisters, 25 years ago, the Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues was established. We were welcomed into this house, not as stakeholders, but as peoples. Over the years, this forum has contributed to shape historic global milestones. It contributed to the path that led to the adoption of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. It informed the 2014 World Conference on Indigenous Peoples. and it continues to strengthen Indigenous peoples' participation across the United Nations system. This forum has consistently elevated what the world too often ignored. It has brought visibility to the crisis of Indigenous peoples' languages, affirmed the rights and leadership of Indigenous women and girls, and ensure that Indigenous peoples' voices are not only present but heard in international decision-making. Many of the mechanisms that exist today within the United Nations system began as recommendations from this very forum. We opened this session with high level participation, including the Secretary General of the United Nations and many member states. I wish to thank and recognize her Excellency Mary Simon, Governor General of Canada, whose presence reminded us that indigenous leadership has helped shaped these spaces. But above all, I thank you, Indigenous delegates and representatives, for your presence, for your perseverance, for your unwavering commitment to the dignity and rights of our peoples. We have reason to feel proud because this forum is an expression of you. It listens to your demands, it carries your concerns, and it elevates your solutions. The forum is a unique global platform that brings together indigenous peoples from the seven socio-cultural regions, member states, and UN entities to advance collective understanding and promotes, upholds, and defends the rights of indigenous peoples. Now, More than ever, in the context of the UN liquidity crisis and the UN80 initiative, we must express our deep concerns about the negative impacts these system-wide constraints are having on the forum. These challenges are not the result of any single office. but rather reflect broader institutional decisions and resource limitations that are beyond the control of those directly supporting the Forum's work. We are witnessing a reduction in our formal session time, a shortening of our report, and significant limitations of formal interpretation services. Reductions in secretariat staffing, driven by higher level decisions, are also having a detrimental impact on our ability to carry out our mandate effectively. Last week, the forum was held in conference room three, which proved inadequate for the level of participation. Indigenous peoples were standing in the stairway without seating. For many, This created a sense of exclusion and raised concerns about the forum's future within this institution. These developments risk undermining the integrity, inclusivity, and effectiveness of this important platform, and we urge that they be addressed at the appropriate levels. I look around this room. I call upon those listening through the webcast. And I implore you to pay special attention to how the UNAD initiative and UN liquidity crisis are negatively impacting the important work of the forum. Join us with a steadfast commitment to protect this space. The special theme of this session, ensuring Indigenous peoples' health, including in the context of conflict, has guided our reflections. We have spoken clearly. There is no health without land. The well-being of Indigenous peoples is inseparable from our lands, waters, and territories. Yet, the health disparities we face are not accidental. They are the result of colonization, dispossession, extractive industries, environmental contamination, and the criminalization of our cultures and healing practices. They are the result of systems imposed without our consent, of children taken from their families, of governance structures dismantled, of treaties violated. To restore health, we must advance decolonization. To guarantee well-being, we must uphold self-determination. Member states have a responsibility to act. Policies must prevent these injustices. The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples must guide all efforts everywhere without exception. During this session, we also held a high-level dialogue on indigenous peoples and climate change, grounded in the rights affirmed in the UN declaration. We heard clearly that Indigenous peoples are facing the most severe and often irreversible impacts of climate change, despite contributing the least to its causes. For us, climate change is not a distant threat. It is a present and lived human rights crisis. We also note the significance of the 2025 advisory opinions of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights and the International Court of Justice. These affirm that Indigenous peoples are not among not only among the most affected, but are essential rights holders and knowledge holders in climate governance. I underscore A message that was echoed strongly throughout this session. There is an urgent need to protect indigenous leaders and indigenous human rights defenders. Their protection is not optional. It is an obligation. Too many continue to face threats, criminalization, and violence for defending their lands, their cultures and their peoples. I acknowledge the great courage and vision of Indigenous leaders and Indigenous human rights defenders. Over the past two weeks, powerful voices have risen from across the seven social cultural regions. And although conditions were not always adequate, I could see the flexibility and patience of Indigenous peoples, attributes we so often have to invoke. As I looked out at the room, I was so inspired to see well-known, long-time Indigenous leaders sharing the space with those who may have joined for the first time. I could hear the clarity and conviction in the statements delivered by Indigenous youth. As we look forward to 20 years of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, I am reminded that this forum is not only about legacy, but it is about our hope and our future. If you did not have the opportunity to speak during the formal sessions, I offer my sincere apologies. But know this, your presence mattered. Your participation in more than 60 side events, your dialogues with foreign members, states, and United Nations representatives, these have shaped this session in meaningful ways. These exchanges are essential. More than a century ago, our ancestors believed that multilateralism could offer a path towards justice. Today, it is our responsibility to make that belief real. As we close this 25th session of the Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues, I extend my deepest gratitude to all of you. I would like to give a special thanks to the colleagues in the document management section who have managed to process and issue our L documents in short time. I would like to thank the interpreters, the sound engineers, conference officers, and others involved in working to make this session a success. I acknowledge and thank my my colleagues, independent experts from all seven social cultural regions who sit as the permanent forum members. I thank them for their tireless efforts in ensuring the successful conclusion of this session. And as many of you know, this year, 11 out of 16 are new members. So I give you a heartfelt congratulations. We have completed your first session. I would like, on behalf of the members of the Forum, to express our gratitude to our colleagues from the Secretariat. In this connection, I wish to thank our colleagues in the Indigenous Peoples and Development Branch of the Division for Inclusive Social Development of DESA for their invaluable support in preparation of and throughout the session. You are few in number, but such a mighty team that work with your full heart to support our forum. Thank you so very much. I also thank the General Assembly and Indigenous Affairs Division in the Department for General Assembly and Conference Management for their support. To Indigenous peoples, to Member States, To our partners across the United Nations system and beyond, thank you very much. May you travel home safely, carrying not only the experience of these past two weeks, the strength of our shared purpose, and the recommitment to protect our space as a forum. May your paths be guided by wisdom, renewed commitment, and the enduring spirit of your peoples. Thank you. Now, what we've all been waiting for, I declare closed the 25th session of the Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues.
